question: We're playing best of five games to 11. In the third game, when do we switch ends?

answer.reasoning: The question is about the best-of-5-games-to-11 format, so the Alternative Laws format 'best-of-5-games-11' applies. Its Clause 8.1.3 directly answers when ends change in the third game: at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game — not mid-game at a score. The standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 Clause 8.1.3 (third game at 11 points) applies to the standard best-of-3-to-21 match, so per the rules I state the standard rule first, then the alternative format rule. The sources fully answer the question; no refusal needed.
answer.answer: Under the standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 (in force 2025-04-26), players change ends "in the third game when a side first scores 11 points, except in Handicap Matches (BWF Statute Section 4.1.3)" [laws-8.1.3]. However, for the format you are playing — best of five games to 11 — the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0, format best-of-5-games-11 (in force 2027-01-04), change this: in the third game you do not switch ends mid-game; you change ends "at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game" [alt-best-of-5-games-11:8.1.3]. So in your third game, you switch ends only when the third game finishes, and only if a fourth game is going to be played.

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question asks when a rally is replayed and for every let situation. Laws 14.1 and 14.3 explain who calls a let and what happens after a let; Laws 14.2 and its subclauses 14.2.1–14.2.7 list the let situations, with 14.2.3 expanded by 14.2.3.1–14.2.3.2. ITTO 5.9.1.2 adds a limit: a shuttle from an adjacent court is not automatically a let. Together these answer the question from the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, plus Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26.
answer.answer: A rally is replayed when a ‘let’ occurs: ‘When a ‘let’ occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again.’ A ‘let’ is called to halt play by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire. Under Law 14.2, it is a let if: (1) the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4); (2) during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted; (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is caught on the net and remains suspended on its top, or after passing over the net is caught in the net; (4) during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle; (5) in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach; (6) a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision; or (7) any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred. Separately, the umpire instructions say a shuttle coming onto the court from an adjacent court is not automatically a let and no let is called if, in the umpire’s opinion, it has not obstructed or distracted the players.

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The sources directly answer both parts of the question. itto-5.14.2 covers a blood-flowing injury and states when the delay ends; itto-3.6.1.4 gives the Referee's time expectation; itto-5.14.1 covers who comes on court (Referee, Tournament Doctor) and that the Umpire times the delay; itto-3.6.1.3 gives the maximum number of persons allowed on court to assist and the fairness requirement for the opposing side. Together they answer what was asked, so no refusal is needed and no further search is required.
answer.answer: For a bleeding (blood flowing) injury, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise [itto-5.14.2]. There is no fixed number of minutes in these sources: the Referee must resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so play can be resumed or abandoned, and may point to potential disqualification if the player is suspected of exploiting the injury to regain wind or repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon [itto-3.6.1.4]. No treatment causing undue delay may be given on court, and the Umpire times the delay caused by the injury [itto-5.14.1]. As for who may come on court: the Umpire calls the Referee onto court if necessary, and the Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required; the Tournament Doctor examines the player and advises on the severity of the injury [itto-5.14.1]. Separately, the Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation, and in fairness must allow the opposing side the same consideration [itto-3.6.1.3]. All of these come from the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26.

citations.quote: For a blood flowing injury, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise.

The Referee shall resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned. The Referee may need to point to potential disqualification if it is suspected that the player is exploiting the injury situation to regain wind, or if the player repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon play.

The Umpire must try to determine the severity of the problem as quickly as possible and call the Referee onto court, if necessary. The Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court (Instruction 3.6). The Tournament Doctor shall examine the player and advise the player about the severity of injury or sickness. No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court. The Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury.

The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation. In fairness, the Referee shall allow the opposing side the same consideration.

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to a match and its score when water makes the court unplayable mid-game. The given sources cover this directly: itto-5.11.3 covers a court that is 'temporarily not playable' during a match, itto-5.11.2 covers suspension for circumstances affecting playing conditions, itto-5.11.4 covers the suspension call and notation, and itto-5.11.5 covers resumption. A search additionally found laws-16.3.3, which answers the score part explicitly: the existing score stands. Together these fully answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: The match is suspended, not restarted, and the score stands exactly where it was. Because a court that is temporarily not playable is a circumstance affecting playing conditions, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play shall be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play [itto-5.11.3, Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.11.3: "If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play."]. Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire when warranted by such a circumstance [itto-5.11.2: "Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions."]. When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call "Play is suspended" and note "S" on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used [itto-5.11.4]. On the score: under Law 16.3.3 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, "If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point." When play resumes, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension, ensure the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call "Are you ready?" followed by the score and "Play" [itto-5.11.5]. So the dripping water stops play temporarily; once the court is again suitable, the same score continues.

citations.quote: If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.
Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions.
When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.
If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.

When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question is directly answered by itto-5.9.1.6, which covers a player throwing sweat or contaminating the court, and by the Laws it points to (Law 16.7 and its sub-clauses 16.7.1.1–16.7.1.3 and 16.7.2), which I read in full to get the complete list of sanctions. The court-wiping instructions (itto-5.4.11, itto-5.10.4) are also relevant to cleaning up the sweat. All sources are from the standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) / ITTO 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26; no Alternative Laws format applies here.
answer.answer: The umpire shall remind the player that throwing sweat / contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings is unacceptable, and apply Law 16.7 if necessary (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.9.1.6). Under Law 16.7.1 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2)), the umpire administers a breach of Law 16.6 (misconduct) by: issuing a warning to the offending side (16.7.1.1); faulting the offending side if previously warned (16.7.1.2); or faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach (16.7.1.3). If the umpire faults the side under 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3, the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who has the power to disqualify the offending side from the match (Law 16.7.2). Separately, the court can be wiped: at the start of each interval the umpire requests Court Attendants/Line Judges to wipe the court (ITTO Clause 5.4.11), and if the court needs wiping the players indicate to the Court Attendants where mopping is needed and must be back on court as soon as the wiping is over (ITTO Clause 5.10.4).

citations.quote: A player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied, if necessary; and
issuing a warning to the offending side; or
faulting the offending side, if previously warned; or
faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach.
On faulting a side (Law 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3), the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match
At the start of each interval (Law 16.2.1), request the Court Attendants/Line Judges to wipe the court.

If the court needs to be wiped, the players shall indicate to the Court Attendants where mopping is needed. The players shall be on court as soon as the wiping is over and before the Court Attendants leave the court.

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question is about a line judge being unsighted on an in/out line call. The relevant sources are ITTO 8.5/8.8 (line judge unsighted signal), ITTO 5.8.3 and 5.8.3.1–5.8.3.3 (umpire takes over when a line judge is unsighted), ITTO 2.5 and Laws 17.6.6 (umpire carries out the unsighted official’s duties or plays a let), Laws 14.2.6 (let if line judge unsighted and umpire/IRS cannot decide), and Laws 14.1/14.3 (what a let does to the rally). Together they answer the question: the rally is decided by the umpire/IRS if possible; only if no decision can be made is it a let, and then the rally since the last service does not count and is replayed.
answer.answer: The line judge must signal immediately that they are unsighted: ITTO 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, says “If unsighted, inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes,” and lists “UNSIGHTED” among the approved hand signals. The rally is not automatically a let. Under ITTO 7.0 (5), “Where there is no Line Judge or if a Line Judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately call” “Out” if the shuttle landed outside the line (then the score or “Service over” and then the score), or the score/“Service over” and then the score if it landed “in”; if the Umpire is also unsighted, the Umpire calls “Let” followed by the score, except that with IRS in operation the Umpire calls “Unsighted” and requests a decision from the system. This matches Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26: Law 17.6.6 says that where an appointed official is unsighted the umpire shall “carry out that official’s duties or play a ‘let’,” and Law 14.2.6 makes it a let if “a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision.” ITTO 2.5 adds that when another official is unsighted the Umpire makes the decision, and when no decision can be made a let is called unless IRS is in use, in which case IRS decides the line call. If a let is called, Law 14.1 says “‘Let’ shall be called by the umpire … to halt play,” and Law 14.3 says “When a ‘let’ occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again.” So: if the umpire or IRS can decide in/out, that call decides the rally; if neither can decide, the umpire calls a let and the rally is replayed from the last service.

The approved hand signals are: SHUTTLE IS OUT SHUTTLE IS IN UNSIGHTED
Where there is no Line Judge or if a Line Judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately call:
“Out” when the shuttle lands outside the line and then call either the score or “Service over” and then the score; or

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question is directly answered by itto-5.12.2, which states where coaches must be during a match and the only exception. Laws 16.2.1 and 16.2.2 define the permitted intervals referenced by that exception, so they are included to state the condition together with the value. No alternative-format rule is needed because the question is about ordinary play, not a best-of-3-games-21 or best-of-5-games-11 format.
answer.answer: No. During the match your coach must remain seated in the designated seat and must not stand court-side, except during the permitted intervals under Law 16.2. Those intervals are: not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points (except Handicap matches), and not exceeding 120 seconds between games. Separately, if the coach wishes to move to another court, that must be done while the shuttle is not in play.

question: What weight range is allowed for a plastic shuttle, and since our hall gets really hot and stuffy in summer, can we use a special type made for hot weather?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts. (1) Weight of a plastic (non-feathered) shuttle: laws-2.3.3 says a non-feathered shuttle's measurements and weight are as in Laws 2.2.2, 2.2.3 and 2.2.6, with up to 10 per cent variation acceptable because of synthetic materials; laws-2.2.6 gives the base weight of 4.74 to 5.50 grams. Together these answer the weight question. (2) Hot/stuffy conditions: laws-2.4 allows modifications to the specifications with the approval of the Member Association concerned where atmospheric conditions due to altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable, subject to no variation in general design, speed and flight. This directly addresses the hot-weather question. Both parts are answered by the given sources, so no tool calls are needed.
answer.answer: Plastic (non-feathered) shuttle weight: the measurements and weight are the same as for a feathered shuttle — laws-2.3.3 states that for a non-feathered shuttle, "Measurements and weight shall be as in Laws 2.2.2, 2.2.3 and 2.2.6," and Law 2.2.6 gives the weight as "from 4.74 to 5.50 grams." However, "because of the difference in the specific gravity and other properties of synthetic materials in comparison with feathers, a variation of up to 10 per cent shall be acceptable" (laws-2.3.3) — so a plastic shuttle may weigh 4.74–5.50 g with up to 10% variation allowed (i.e., roughly 4.27 g to 6.05 g at the extremes). Hot weather: yes, a special shuttle may be used — Law 2.4 (laws-2.4) provides that "Subject to there being no variation in the general design, speed and flight of the shuttle, modifications in the above specifications may be made with the approval of the Member Association concerned, in places where atmospheric conditions due to either altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable." So for a hot, stuffy hall (a climate condition), you may use a modified shuttle only with the approval of your Member Association, and only if its general design, speed and flight are unchanged. All rules cited are from the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26.

question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts. (1) Whether a pre-'Play' yellow card costs a point now: itto-5.17.10 directly covers misconduct before 'Play' is called and states cards given then have no effect on the score but are taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2). (2) Whether the card goes on record after the tournament: itto-3.7.3 states the Referee must send BWF (or CC) a report on yellow and red cards after the tournament that may trigger further sanctions, and itto-3.7.3.1 adds the Referee may decide not to report a card if they observed it and decide it should not have been issued. Together these answer both parts, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: No, the yellow card does not cost him a point now. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.17.10 (in force 2025-04-26), misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before "Play" has been called is treated as in Instructions 5.17.3, 5.17.4 or 5.17.5, and "Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match but a card(s) shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2)." So the card only matters if he commits further offences during the match — under Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Law 16.7.1.2 (in force 2025-04-26), the umpire faults the offending side "if previously warned". As for the record after the tournament: yes, the card is reported. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 3.7.3 (in force 2025-04-26), "The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions." However, under Clause 3.7.3.1, "The Referee may decide not to report a card given by an Umpire, if the Referee or a Deputy has observed the situation where the card was given and decides that the card should not have been issued."
